palenques is very difficult. While many of the Rivers in Jamaica have retained their former Spanish name, or derivatives of their former Spanish names, there is no known river on current maps, English colonial maps immediately preceding the conquest, or the few Spanish maps available with a river named Juana. This might have been one of the many former rivers or waterways that had dried up, given the prevalence of droughts and prolonged periods with short rainfall in what is now the Clarendon plains. The Palenque de Río Juana is also not referred to again in Spanish sources after reports about the April 3 coalition. The Palenque de Río Juana could have likely been the name of the palenque in Porus, the other in what is now called Bowers Gully, or a different palenque altogether. &#x22;,&#x22;7614889f-3737-4fcb-a3f3-780bef9164c2&#x22;:[{&#x22;id&#x22;:&#x22;75861864-c7e0-4607-9afa-6a33427f3194&#x22;,&#x22;inverse&#x22;:false,&#x22;name&#x22;:&#x22;Clarendon Parish&#x22;,&#x22;name_facet&#x22;:&#x22;Clarendon Parish&#x22;,&#x22;names&#x22;:[&#x22;Clarendon Parish&#x22;],&#x22;names_facet&#x22;:[&#x22;Clarendon Parish&#x22;],&#x22;properties&#x22;:{},&#x22;record_id&#x22;:&#x22;198089&#x22;,&#x22;uuid&#x22;:&#x22;75861864-c7e0-4607-9afa-6a33427f3194&#x22;}],&#x22;88f155dc-daf7-4fa0-8aaf-a8c7bf4ff3d4&#x22;:[{&#x22;4b9767ef-abb3-4ec7-9d0a-1da853ec8740&#x22;:&#x22;1660-01-01&#x22;,&#x22;cbefa9a9-abf9-4eeb-b78d-19f6d6914724&#x22;:&#x22;e001&#x22;,&#x22;d5cf5335-1c56-43f8-aeb0-500267eeac98&#x22;:&#x22;1656-04-03&#x22;,&#x22;end_date&#x22;:[-9782640000,-9782553600],&#x22;end_year&#x22;:[1660,1660],&#x22;end_year_facet&#x22;:[1660,1660],&#x22;id&#x22;:&#x22;4826e8ff-a1ce-44a6-95f9-6cfbf53ed0ac&#x22;,&#x22;inverse&#x22;:false,&#x22;name&#x22;:&#x22;Flight: Palenque de Río Juana&#x22;,&#x22;name_facet&#x22;:&#x22;Flight: Palenque de Río Juana&#x22;,&#x22;record_id&#x22;:&#x22;87668&#x22;,&#x22;start_date&#x22;:[-9929088000,-9929001600],&#x22;start_year&#x22;:[1655,1655],&#x22;start_year_facet&#x22;:[1655,1655],&#x22;uuid&#x22;:&#x22;4826e8ff-a1ce-44a6-95f9-6cfbf53ed0ac&#x22;}],&#x22;all_projects&#x22;:[{&#x22;id&#x22;:237,&#x22;name&#x22;:&#x22;Marronage Mapping Project&#x22;,&#x22;name_facet&#x22;:&#x22;Marronage Mapping Project&#x22;}],&#x22;bfdafc68-a563-4b71-94c3-a00c9e5bc7a9&#x22;:&#x22;In April 1656, don Cristóbal Isasi Arnaldo, then the maestre de campo before being appointed temporary military governor, formed a joint Spanish-Maroon coalition with \&#x22;treinte hombres españoles y quince negros del palenque de Río Juana [...]\&#x22; in an attempt to dislodge the English from the hatos of Guatibacoa near the island's main town. According to another report, these bowmen were among many others: \&#x22;que se han retirado de sus amos y habitan en lugares fuertes que ellos llaman palenques [...].\&#x22; After the brief campaign, the small party returned to Isasi Arnaldo's stronghold in the montes of Manatines, where they distributed the loot amongst themselves. One of the Spanish captains present during this affair claimed that after the maroons took their share, they promised to return upon future occasions in greater numbers. the palenques is very difficult. While many of the Rivers in Jamaica have retained their former Spanish name, or derivatives of their former Spanish names, there is no known river on current maps, English colonial maps immediately preceding the conquest, or the few Spanish maps available with a river named Juana. This might have been one of the many former rivers or waterways that had dried up, given the prevalence of droughts and prolonged periods with short rainfall in what is now the Clarendon plains. The Palenque de Río Juana is also not referred to again in Spanish sources after reports about the April 3 coalition. The Palenque de Río Juana could have likely been the name of the palenque in Porus, the other in what is now called Bowers Gully, or a different palenque altogether. While many of the Rivers in Jamaica have retained their former Spanish name, or derivatives of their former Spanish names, there is no known river on current maps, English colonial maps immediately preceding the conquest, or the few Spanish maps available with a river named Juana. This might have been one of the many former rivers or waterways that had dried up, given the prevalence of droughts and prolonged periods with short rainfall in what is now the Clarendon plains. The Palenque de Río Juana is also not referred to again in Spanish sources after reports about the April 3 coalition. Melvis Campbell suggests that the town existed long before the treaties concluding the first maroon war were drawn. At the same time, contemporary observer Edward Long claims the town was founded by the overflow of survivors from Nanny Town, which the English destroyed in 1733. Both scenarios could also be true. Crawford Town is first mentioned in the treaty the English government signed with Captain Quao, concluding the First Maroon War. In the years following the town's charter after the first Maroon War, the settlements experienced significant internal discord, which culminated in civil conflict, resulting in the town's burning in 1754. Melvis Campbell suggests that the town existed long before the treaties concluding the first maroon war were drawn. At the same time, contemporary observer Edward Long claims the town was founded by the overflow of survivors from Nanny Town, which the English destroyed in 1733. Both scenarios could also be true. Crawford Town is first mentioned in the treaty the English government signed with Captain Quao, concluding the First Maroon War. In the years following the town&#39;s charter after the first Maroon War, the settlements experienced significant internal discord, which culminated in civil conflict, resulting in the town&#39;s burning in 1754. Melvis Campbell suggests that the town existed long before the treaties concluding the first maroon war were drawn. At the same time, contemporary observer Edward Long claims the town was founded by the overflow of survivors from Nanny Town, which the English destroyed in 1733. Both scenarios could also be true. Crawford Town is first mentioned in the treaty the English government signed with Captain Quao, concluding the First Maroon War. In the years following the town&#39;s charter after the first Maroon War, the settlements experienced significant internal discord, which culminated in civil conflict, resulting in the town&#39;s burning in 1754. Melvis Campbell suggests that the town existed long before the treaties concluding the first maroon war were drawn. At the same time, contemporary observer Edward Long claims the town was founded by the overflow of survivors from Nanny Town, which the English destroyed in 1733. Both scenarios could also be true. Crawford Town is first mentioned in the treaty the English government signed with Captain Quao, concluding the First Maroon War. In the years following the town's charter after the first Maroon War, the settlements experienced significant internal discord, which culminated in civil conflict, resulting in the town's burning in 1754. The survivors relocated and founded the Charles Town/New Crawford Town communities that formed in the Blue and John Crow Mountains at the end of the seventeenth century as a result of the English settlements and plantations into the Island's eastern frontier in the parishes of St. Goerge and St. Thomas. In 1686, a report made by the colonial assembly estimated the maroons had been gathering in those parishes for the past fourteen to fifteen years. Guys Town was established by a former plantation headman named \&#x22;Guy\&#x22; at the top of Carrion Crow Hill. A testimony made in 1733 described it as a well planted settlement with \&#x22;sugar cane, cocoa, plantains, yams, melon, and corn, and the hogs, poultry, and grazing cows\&#x22; (Campbell, 1977). It is possible that Guy's Town also incorporated the surviviors from the Shipwreck recorded in 1670 and those who lived dwelled in the island during the Spanish colonial period and fled from the Hatos of Morante and Ayala (Yallahs) during the English conquest of communities that formed in the Blue and John Crow Mountains at the end of the seventeenth century as a result of the English settlements and plantations into the Island's eastern frontier in the parishes of St. Goerge and St. Thomas. In 1686, a report made by the colonial assembly estimated the maroons had been gathering in those parishes for the past fourteen to fifteen years. Guys Town was established by a former plantation headman named \&#x22;Guy\&#x22; at the top of Carrion Crow Hill. A testimony made in 1733 described it as a well planted settlement with \&#x22;sugar cane, cocoa, plantains, yams, melon, and corn, and the hogs, poultry, and grazing cows\&#x22; (Campbell, 1977). It is possible that Guy's Town also incorporated the surviviors from the Shipwreck recorded in 1670 and those who lived dwelled in the island during the Spanish colonial period and fled from the Hatos of Morante and Ayala (Yallahs) during the English conquest of During the first Maroon War (1730-1739), Nanny Town's residents was destroyed in 1732 by English regulars (Kopytoff 1978). Cudjoe town which together formed the Leeward Maroon Complex. The founding inhabitants of this settlement were among the two hundred enslaved African captives who rebelled on the Lobby Plantation and fled into the cockpit country, led by Cudjoe. In the cockpit country, Cudjoe divided the community into an additional group headed by his brother, Accompong, yet still subordinate to Cudjoe. It is unclear specifically when Accompong Town was founded. However, historians believe it was founded sometime during the First Maroon War (1720-1739) as an outpost to facilitate the organization and activities of Maroon raiding In the cockpit country, Cudjoe divided the community into an additional group headed by his brother, Accompong, yet still subordinate to Cudjoe. It is unclear specifically when Accompong Town was founded. However, historians believe it was founded sometime during the First Maroon War (1720-1739) as an outpost to facilitate the organization and activities of Maroon raiding In the cockpit country, Cudjoe divided the community into an additional group headed by his brother, Accompong, yet still subordinate to Cudjoe. Mapping Project&#x22;,&#x22;name_facet&#x22;:&#x22;Marronage Mapping Project&#x22;}],&#x22;bfdafc68-a563-4b71-94c3-a00c9e5bc7a9&#x22;:&#x22;This settlement was founded by two hundred enslaved African captives who rebelled on the Lobby Plantation in 1673 and fled into the cockpit country. They were joined by another two hundred enslaved people who revolted on the Sutton plantation in 1690 and were led by an Akan Chieftain, whose son, Captain Cudjoe, would govern the polity into the first half of the eighteenth century (Kopytoff 1978). In the Eighteenth century, this and other maroon polities that broke away from Cudjoe's chain of command in the Cockpit country were referred to as the Leeward Maroons. In the 1730s, the English launched a decade-long armed struggle against the Leeward and Windward Maroons, known as the First Maroon War. In 1739, the Leeward Maroons’ successful resistance against the English forced the Colonial government to sue for peace, chartered Cudjoe Town as a free \&#x22;maroon town,” and grant them 1,500 acres of land. In 1739, following the conclusion of the first Maroon War and chartering of the town, Colonial officials estimated that Leeward Maroon's population was 470 people, including women and children. As the population estimate referred to the \&#x22;leeward Maroons,\&#x22; it is unclear if this computation included Accompong Town or if it solely referred to Cudjoe's hundred enslaved African captives who rebelled on the Lobby Plantation in 1673 and fled into the cockpit country. They were joined by another two hundred enslaved people who revolted on the Sutton plantation in 1690 and were led by an Akan Chieftain, whose son, Captain Cudjoe, would govern the polity into the first half of the eighteenth century (Kopytoff 1978). In the Eighteenth century, this and other maroon polities that broke away from Cudjoe&#39;s chain of command in the Cockpit country were referred to as the Leeward Maroons. In the 1730s, the English launched a decade-long armed struggle against the Leeward and Windward Maroons, known as the First Maroon War. In 1739, the Leeward Maroons’ successful resistance against the English forced the Colonial government to sue for peace, chartered Cudjoe Town as a free &quot;maroon town,” and grant them 1,500 acres of land. In 1739, following the conclusion of the first Maroon War and chartering of the town, Colonial officials estimated that Leeward Maroon&#39;s population was 470 people, including women and children. As the population estimate referred to the &quot;leeward Maroons,&quot; it is unclear if this computation included Accompong Town or if it solely referred to Cudjoe&#39;s They were joined by another two hundred enslaved people who revolted on the Sutton plantation in 1690 and were led by an Akan Chieftain, whose son, Captain Cudjoe, would govern the polity into the first half of the eighteenth century (Kopytoff 1978). In the Eighteenth century, this and other maroon polities that broke away from Cudjoe&#39;s chain of command in the Cockpit country were referred to as the Leeward Maroons. In the 1730s, the English launched a decade-long armed struggle against the Leeward and Windward Maroons, known as the First Maroon War. In 1739, the Leeward Maroons’ successful resistance against the English forced the Colonial government to sue for peace, chartered Cudjoe Town as a free &quot;maroon town,” and grant them 1,500 acres of land. In 1739, following the conclusion of the first Maroon War and chartering of the town, Colonial officials estimated that Leeward Maroon&#39;s population was 470 people, including women and children. in a report made in 1659 that claims that three palenques had been successfully reduced under the obedience of the Spanish. That same year, an English party endeavoring to seek out the hidden locations of Jamaica’s maroon enclaves discovered Lubolo’s settlement and described it as a settled town with 200 acres of planted provisions. To prevent the English party from destroying the town, Juan Lubolo and his officers negotiated a commissioned alliance with the English, wherein they agreed to lead the English to the hidden Spanish strongholds on the northern coast and the other maroon palenques. After the expulsion of the Spanish, the English formerly granted the community English subjecthood, individual land grants, and, for Juan Lubolo, the title of colonel of the Black Regiment in 1662. By the 1680s, most of the members that belonged to the Palenque lost their land titles to expanding sugar planters and relocated to Santiago de la Vega, then renamed Spanish town. Recent scholarship has also suggested that some of those belonging to this community emigrated to Veracruz New Spain. That same year, an English party endeavoring to seek out the hidden locations of Jamaica’s maroon enclaves discovered Lubolo’s settlement and described it as a settled town with 200 acres of planted provisions. To prevent the English party from destroying the town, Juan Lubolo and his officers negotiated a commissioned alliance with the English, wherein they agreed to lead the English to the hidden Spanish strongholds on the northern coast and the other maroon palenques. After the expulsion of the Spanish, the English formerly granted the community English subjecthood, individual land grants, and, for Juan Lubolo, the title of colonel of the Black Regiment in 1662. By the 1680s, most of the members that belonged to the Palenque lost their land titles to expanding sugar planters and relocated to Santiago de la Vega, then renamed Spanish town. Recent scholarship has also suggested that some of those belonging to this community emigrated to Veracruz New Spain. appears indirectly in a report made in 1659 that claims that three palenques had been successfully reduced under the obedience of the Spanish. That same year, an English party endeavoring to seek out the hidden locations of Jamaica’s maroon enclaves discovered Lubolo’s settlement and described it as a settled town with 200 acres of planted provisions. To prevent the English party from destroying the town, Juan Lubolo and his officers negotiated a commissioned alliance with the English, wherein they agreed to lead the English to the hidden Spanish strongholds on the northern coast and the other maroon palenques. After the expulsion of the Spanish, the English formerly granted the community English subjecthood, individual land grants, and, for Juan Lubolo, the title of colonel of the Black Regiment in 1662. By the 1680s, most of the members that belonged to the Palenque lost their land titles to expanding sugar planters and relocated to Santiago de la Vega, then renamed Spanish town. Recent scholarship has also suggested that some of those belonging to this community emigrated to Veracruz New Spain. in a report made in 1659 that claims that three palenques had been successfully reduced under the obedience of the Spanish. That same year, an English party endeavoring to seek out the hidden locations of Jamaica’s maroon enclaves discovered Lubolo’s settlement and described it as a settled town with 200 acres of planted provisions. To prevent the English party from destroying the town, Juan Lubolo and his officers negotiated a commissioned alliance with the English, wherein they agreed to lead the English to the hidden Spanish strongholds on the northern coast and the other maroon palenques. After the expulsion of the Spanish, the English formerly granted the community English subjecthood, individual land grants, and, for Juan Lubolo, the title of colonel of the Black Regiment in 1662. By the 1680s, most of the members that belonged to the Palenque lost their land titles to expanding sugar planters and relocated to Santiago de la Vega, then renamed Spanish town. Recent scholarship has also suggested that some of those belonging to this community emigrated to Veracruz New Spain. of the maroon community in Vermejales, comprised of over 200 formerly enslaved men and women. Like the Porus settlement, this community accommodated the Spanish to gain access to clothes and other necessities in exchange for cultivated cassava and hunts they provided the Spanish with. During the breakdown of negotiations between the Spanish and English in 1660, informed the English that the Palenque governed headed by a chief named Juan de Seras in light of the death of an English negotiator who went to the community to discuss terms under the assumption that the community was incorporated under Spanish rule. Despite repeated attempts to treat the community following the expulsion of the Spanish during the first two decades of English colonial rule, the community continued to pose resistance against the expansion of English colonial settlement on the island’s northern side. It is unclear what happened to the community. Some accounts claimed that the community fused with the new emergent fugitive communities that fled from English plantations, while other sources claimed that they had fled the island. gaining the support of the maroon community in Vermejales, comprised of over 200 formerly enslaved men and women. Like the Porus settlement, this community accommodated the Spanish to gain access to clothes and other necessities in exchange for cultivated cassava and hunts they provided the Spanish with. During the breakdown of negotiations between the Spanish and English in 1660, informed the English that the Palenque governed headed by a chief named Juan de Seras in light of the death of an English negotiator who went to the community to discuss terms under the assumption that the community was incorporated under Spanish rule. Despite repeated attempts to treat the community following the expulsion of the Spanish during the first two decades of English colonial rule, the community continued to pose resistance against the expansion of English colonial settlement on the island’s northern side. It is unclear what happened to the community. Some accounts claimed that the community fused with the new emergent fugitive communities that fled from English plantations, while other sources claimed that they had fled the island. of the maroon community in Vermejales, comprised of over 200 formerly enslaved men and women. Like the Porus settlement, this community accommodated the Spanish to gain access to clothes and other necessities in exchange for cultivated cassava and hunts they provided the Spanish with. During the breakdown of negotiations between the Spanish and English in 1660, informed the English that the Palenque governed headed by a chief named Juan de Seras in light of the death of an English negotiator who went to the community to discuss terms under the assumption that the community was incorporated under Spanish rule. Despite repeated attempts to treat the community following the expulsion of the Spanish during the first two decades of English colonial rule, the community continued to pose resistance against the expansion of English colonial settlement on the island’s northern side. It is unclear what happened to the community. Some accounts claimed that the community fused with the new emergent fugitive communities that fled from English plantations, while other sources claimed that they had fled the island. In exchange for their armsmen, hunters, provision fields, and the use of their settlements as stronghold points in the fight against the English, the Spanish provided them with clothes, manufactured and the promise of freedom. This settlement was one of three maroon communities with whom the Spanish governor brokered an alliance. In exchange for their armsmen, hunters, provision fields, and the use of their settlements as stronghold points in the fight against the English, the Spanish provided them with clothes, manufactured and the promise of freedom. In early 1660, Juan Lubolo’s party raided the settlement and captured between fifty and sixty members of the community. Doyley mention that the settlement included extensive provision grounds. The subsequent encounter resulted in capturing the provison grounds used to provide for the English troops and the dispersal of its surviving inhabitants. The editors of the published transcription of one of the reports detailing this encounter note that &quot;the provision field that was discovered was probably situated on the banks of Bowyers Gully above the reservoir now serving Old Harbor. This site brings together settlement records, events, and primary sources into a searchable, map-centered interface. Use the **Places** tab to browse settlements, **Events** to follow the historical record over time, and **Paths** to walk through curated narratives that connect places.

Posts like this one share project updates, methodological notes, and short essays from the research team. We'll be publishing regularly as the dataset grows.
